articles.title_orig: Stocks tumble as investors take profits following blockbuster Anthropic IPO: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks tumble as investors take profits following blockbuster Anthropic IPO: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks tumbled on Thursday, falling to their lows of the session the very moment the widely anticipated artificial intelligence IPO Anthropic began trading .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 1.7% after gaining as much as 2% earlier in the session. The S&P 500 shed 1.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 920 points, or 1.8%.
Anthropic , trading at the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, opened shortly before noon at $111.50 per share, a 34% pop. The stock was trading more than 10% off the first trading price and was last up 14%.
The major averages fell to session lows immediately following the start of trading for the much-hyped IPO, as investors appeared to take profits at the culmination of this moment for the AI trade.
The artificial intelligence company priced its initial public offering at $83 a share, above the expected range. That had chip stocks and other AI plays jumping in morning trading.
Chipmakers Nvidia and Micron Technology gave up their gains, along with tech giants Microsoft and Meta Platforms . Advanced Micro Devices lost more than 8% after Hunterbrook Capital disclosed a short position in the name, pointing to alleged U.S. export control breaches that involve China.
"This was always going to be a critical test for the tech sector. Anthropic could be the new poster child for AI trade, especially after Nvidia headlines," said Aleks Spencer, Bogart Wealth CIO. "There's a lot here too that needs to be processed and digested, which translates to this period of uncertainty and volatility."
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) , or Wall Street's so-called fear gauge, reached a day high of close to 29 — its highest level since March — shortly after Anthropic began trading and investors moved out of tech stocks. The index was last above 27.
"The enthusiasm comes in, and it's a great moment to sell the rally and take some profits," Spencer added.
The market has become more cautious on AI as of late, with investors focusing on whether heavy spending on the buildout will translate into meaningful profits. The iShares AI Innovation and Tech Active ETF (BAI) has fallen 10% this month, and embattled AI bellwether Nvidia has dropped 27% while the company grapples with the resignation of its CEO Jensen Huang. Shares of CoreWeave, which had seen its bond yields trade above 16% earlier this month, is down 16% in November.
To be sure, some on Wall Street aren't too alarmed about the rollercoaster ride sparked by Anthropic's debut.
"Today doesn't matter," said Baird tech strategist Ted Mortonson, who deemed the day's action in Anthropic akin to that of a casino. "It's a blink of an eye of their journey. It's an important event, but how they navigate the next three years that will determine valuation."
While the major indexes took a leg lower immediately after Anthropic began trading at the Nasdaq, Interactive Brokers' chief strategist Steve Sosnick noted that the premarket rally faded before the artificial intelligence giant began trading.
"What we saw before that was the latest round of 'sell the rally' trading that has overtaken the more customary 'buy the dip' in recent days," he said.
Sosnick said that the rationale for the drop wasn't clear, though once the S&P 500 was able to break through a key support level in recent days, 7,300, that's when selling accelerated.
"The dam seemed to break once the big event was behind us," he added.
The Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) topped 27 on Thursday, signaling uncertainty in the U.S. market.
It was last hovering at 27.94.
The stock market has been volatile as of late as investors have priced in macreconomic and geopolitical uncertainty. On Thursday, Anthropic listed its shares on the Nasdaq, sparking a selloff that rattled many areas of the market.
The S&P 500 fell further below its 200-day moving average on Thursday as stocks sold off following Anthropic 's initial public offering.
The broad-market index was last hovering around 7,273.98. That puts it about 74 points, or roughly 1%, below its 200-day moving average of 7,348.54.
"That's a big technical signal," Thomas Martin, a partner and senior portfolio manager at Globalt Investments, told CNBC. "It has been above its 200-day moving average for a long time. And, if you're a trend follower, you say, 'okay, well, maybe if it breaks through, you have room to the downside.'"
The S&P 500's latest decline comes one day after its closed below its 200-day moving average for the first time since April 7.
Stocks rolled over to session lows nearly immediately after Anthropic began trading at the Nasdaq. While the AI giant opened 34% higher, it quickly eased from those levels — as enthusiasm around the company's public market debut withered.
The Dow tumbled to trade more than 1,000 points lower, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite were down more than 1% each.
The declines put the Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq all down more than 3% for the month. Per Bespoke, this would be the first November since 2008 that all major indexes are down that much through Nov. 18.
Shares in frontier artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic opened at $111.50, up 34.3% from its $83 initial public offering price, after raising a record $81 billion in the largest ever sale of stock by a company entering the public market for the first time.
At the opening price, Anthropic, led by CEO Dario Amodei, has a fully diluted market capitalization of roughly $2 trillion. San Francisco-based Anthropic trades on the Nasdaq Stock Market under ticker symbol ANT.
Amodei co-founded Anthropic less than six years ago, in 2021, alongside a handful of other researchers after the group collectively defected from OpenAI.
— Scott Schnipper, Ashley Capoot and Leslie Picker
Anthropic's debut on Thursday will serve as a key measure of just how much investors remain bullish on the artificial intelligence trade.
"It'll be an important barometer for investors' AI appetite," said Callie Cox, director of investment strategy at Plancorp. "AI stocks desperately need some wind at their backs, too ... Wall Street needs a sign that investors still believe in the potential for AI beyond already-elevated expectations."
"The challenge in that thesis is that hot IPOs rarely perform well right out of the gate, especially these days, when every company seems to be vying for a limited pool of capital to fund their AI strategy," she said. "While I wouldn't be surprised to see the stock market take cues from Anthropic's performance, I'd caution investors about trying to read the tea leaves from one event too much."
Enthusiasm around the Anthropic IPO is lifting the broader tech trade, especially those stocks that are direct proxies for the AI company. Here are the latest moves:
JPMorgan downgraded Alphabet corporate bonds to neutral from overweight, noting that "tighter valuations leave less room for outperformance relative to Amazon."
"Our base case assumes strong growth and eventual improvement in cash conversion, but [free cash flow] remains negative through 2028, requiring further financing while substantial liquidity and earnings keep leverage low," wrote credit analyst Erica Spear. "Alphabet's quarter exposed a widening divergence between accelerating Cloud demand and slowing Search growth, with weaker monetization of AI queries adding to uncertainty around the core earnings engine."
The three major averages began Thursday's session in positive territory.
The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.5% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 gained 1%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 230 points, or 0.4%.
U.S. gold futures for December delivery hit a low of $3,694.5 on Thursday, before recovering slightly to back above $3,700.
The low represented a level that the metal hasn't traded at since September 2025.
Gold is currently down 4.4% on the week, and tracking for its second straight weekly loss and the fifth negative one in six. The VanEck Gold Miners ETF (GDX) was down 1% in premarket trading Thursday.
— Gina Francolla and Davis Giangiulio

articles.title_orig: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.title_zh: Israeli military completes ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.content_orig:
Israeli forces have completed a rare ground operation in part of central Gaza outside their control, the military says, a day after residents were ordered to evacuate.
Families fled their homes and tents on Wednesday as tanks advanced into an area east of Nuseirat refugee camp and onto the territory's main north-south road under the cover of artillery strikes.
The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.
The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire deal.
Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.
Wednesday's Israeli incursion deep beyond the Yellow Line was reportedly the first to be publicly announced by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since the ceasefire began.
In the early afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the operation and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety. It also said a section of Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.
In the evening, the IDF said the joint operation with the Shin Bet security service sought "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".
On Thursday morning, Cogat told Palestinians on social media that "the activity has ended, and the Salah al-Din axis has been reopened".
Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".
Gaza's Hamas-run government media office meanwhile said that an estimated 6,000 people had fled their homes and tents because of the operation, and that this amounted to the war crime of forced displacement.
Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed dozens of families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the Israeli evacuation order.
In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man could be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he said.
An image, meanwhile, showed six armoured vehicles, including tanks and bulldozers, around Salah al-Din road.
A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."
"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."
A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".
Asked about those reports, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.
Multiple verified videos of the aftermath of the incursion on Thursday showed destruction, earth banks, and heavy vehicle tracks more than 1.2km beyond the Yellow Line.
That is believed to be the furthest Israeli troops have advanced into central Gaza since they occupied the so-called Netzarim Corridor before the ceasefire.
Some residents returned to check their properties following the Israeli withdrawal.
"The entire area has been destroyed, and we honestly do not know what to do," Abd Aliwa told Reuters news agency as he sat beside a pile of rubble.
Gaza's Hamas-run Civil Defence agency said three people were killed and others were wounded in three separate Israeli drone strikes on Wednesday.
One man was killed in Nuseirat, the second was killed to the north in Gaza City, and the third was killed in the central town of Deir al-Balah, it added.
The IDF told the BBC that it had "struck several military operatives".
Gaza health officials said another two people were killed on Thursday by Israeli fire in eastern Gaza City, according to Reuters. There was no immediate comment from the IDF.
At least 1,662 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the ceasefire began last year, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The Israeli military says six of its soldiers have been killed over the same period.
Meanwhile, more than 1.9 million people - about 90% of Gaza's population - remain displaced, with 1.4 million of them living in tents or makeshift shelters, according to the UN.
Reconstruction has yet to begin in Gaza, where an estimated 82% of all structures have been destroyed or damaged during the war, as US President Donald Trump's peace plan has largely stalled.
The disarmament of Hamas has been a key sticking point.
The group has agreed to give up its weapons in exchange for a phased withdrawal of Israeli troops from the 60% of Gaza they currently occupy. But Israel has insisted that Hamas must fully disarm before any pullout.
The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,710 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, its health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says
articles.title_zh: There is no going back ‘to the way it was before’ the Iran war’s energy shock, IEA says
articles.content_orig:
The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ⁠ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
Energy markets have been rattled this year by the conflict, which has curbed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz , a route that ⁠typically carries about a fifth of global oil and ​liquefied natural ⁠gas supplies and is a key artery for Gulf exports.
“In my view, the energy world will never be the same again as it was before the Iran ⁠war,” IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said in an interview alongside the release of the agency’s World ​Energy ⁠Outlook 2026.
The conflict has resulted in cumulative ‌losses of 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas supplies from the Gulf, the Paris-based agency said.
The annual outlook includes a range of scenarios based on existing and ‌proposed energy policies. This year it also examines how governments ‌and markets could respond to prolonged disruption in Hormuz.
Under a new Additional Response Case (ARC), the IEA said energy security concerns could speed up electrification, energy-efficiency measures and efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels.
In that case, global oil demand in 2035 ⁠is 4.4 million barrels per day lower than under the agency’s Stated Policies Scenario (STEPS), which reflects governments’ current policy intentions. Electric vehicles alone would displace more than 11 million bpd of oil demand.
Global oil demand falls to 97 million bpd in 2035 and 85 million bpd by 2050 under ARC, compared with just over 101 million bpd in 2035 under STEPS
Gas demand under ARC is more than 300 bcm lower than under STEPS.
The report said electrification is now cost-competitive across large parts of transport, ‌heating and industry, although inadequate grids, charging networks and power supplies could slow its rollout.
“Many ​countries are seeing electrification as a policy option for energy security. Instead of importing energy, ‌they decided to build energy at home,” Birol ⁠said.
Electricity’s share of final energy consumption is projected to approach 30% globally under STEPS, ⁠up from about 23% today, as transport, heating and parts of industry switch away from fossil fuels.
Alongside data centers, rising demand ‌for cooling is emerging as one ​of the strongest drivers of electricity consumption. For the ‌first time, demand for cooling in buildings has ​exceeded demand for heating, the IEA said, as higher temperatures and rising incomes drive rapid growth in air-conditioner use.

Mortgage rates moved higher this week, ending a four-week streak of declines, as bond investors grew more nervous about inflation.
The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate was 7.28% this week through Wednesday, according to Freddie Mac data, up from 7.11% a week earlier.
Mortgage News Daily, which uses different data to calculate rates, put the average mortgage rate at 7.46% as of Wednesday, up from 7.18% at the beginning of last week.
The jump came after the 10-year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates closely track, moved higher last week after inflation data for consumer and producer prices came in hotter than expected, cementing odds that the Federal Reserve will hike benchmark interest rates at its December meeting.
The Fed doesn't directly control mortgage rates, but expectations about the central bank's future actions influence their direction.
"The debate has shifted from whether the Fed hikes in December to how aggressively it moves ," Realtor.com senior economist Anthony Smith said in a statement. "That is a tough backdrop for mortgage rates heading into what is already a seasonally slow stretch for the housing market."
Here are the current purchase mortgage rates for today, Thursday, November 19, 2026 , according to the latest Zillow data:
Here are the current refinance mortgage rates for today, Thursday, November 19, 2026 , according to the latest Zillow data:
Use Yahoo Finance's mortgage calculator below to see how various mortgage rates will impact your monthly payments and overall loan costs.
Bookmark the Yahoo Finance mortgage payment calculator and keep it handy as you shop for homes and lenders. Be sure to use the dropdown to include private mortgage insurance costs and HOA dues if they apply to you. These monthly expenses, along with your mortgage principal and interest rate, will give you a realistic idea of your monthly payment.
Two categories determine mortgage rates : those you can control and those you cannot.
What factors can you control? First, you can compare the mortgage lenders to find the one that gives you the lowest rate and fees.
Second, lenders typically extend lower rates to people with higher credit scores, lower debt-to-income (DTI) ratios , and considerable down payments. If you can save more or pay down debt before securing a mortgage, a lender will probably give you a better interest rate.
What factors can you not control? In short, the economy.
The list of ways the economy impacts mortgage rates is long, but here are the basic details. If the economy — for example, employment rates — is struggling, mortgage rates decrease to encourage borrowing, which helps boost the economy. If the economy is strong, mortgage rates go up to temper spending.
With all other factors being equal, mortgage refinance rates are typically slightly higher than purchase rates. So don't be surprised if your refinance rate is higher than you may have expected.
Two of the most common mortgage terms are 30-year and 15-year fixed-rate mortgages . Both lock in your rate for the entire loan term.
A 30-year mortgage is popular because it has relatively low monthly payments. But it comes with a higher interest rate than shorter terms, and because you're accumulating interest for three decades, you'll pay a lot of interest in the long run.
A 15-year mortgage can be a good choice because it has a lower rate than longer terms, so you'll pay less interest over time. You'll also pay off your mortgage much faster. But your monthly payments will be higher because you're paying off the same loan amount in half the time.
Basically, 30-year mortgages are more affordable from month to month, while 15-year mortgages are cheaper in the long run.
According to Yahoo Finance's weekly survey of lenders with the lowest rates , some of the banks with the lowest median mortgage rates are Chase and Citibank . However, it's a good idea to shop around for the best rate, not just with banks, but also with credit unions and companies specializing in mortgage lending.
Yes, 2.75% is an amazing mortgage rate. You're unlikely to get a 2.75% rate in today's market unless you take on an assumable mortgage from a seller who locked in this rate in 2020 or 2021, when rates were at all-time lows.
According to Freddie Mac, the lowest-ever 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 2.65%. This was the national average in January 2021. It is extremely unlikely that rates will dip below 3% again anytime soon.
Some experts say it's worth refinancing when you can lock in a rate that's 2% less than your current mortgage rate. Others say 1% is the magic number. It all depends on your financial goals when refinancing, how long you plan to stay in the same house, and on your break-even point after paying the refinance closing costs.

articles.title_orig: Trump presses European leaders about Ukraine aid in call after Putin summit
articles.title_zh: Trump presses European leaders about Ukraine aid in call after Putin summit
articles.content_orig:
BERLIN — U.S. President Donald Trump called in to a meeting of Ukraine’s European allies on Thursday, according to four European officials who were briefed on the discussion, where he sharply questioned their continued spending on military support for Kyiv.
Hours after concluding a meeting with Kremlin chief Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, Trump called Berlin from Air Force One and said the Russian leader was serious about peace negotiations about Ukraine.
On the call, Trump vigorously expressed his skepticism about further billions in aid being provided to Ukraine by the so-called Coalition of the Willing, according to three of the European officials, who were granted anonymity to describe a private meeting.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
When asked at a press conference following the coalition meeting whether Trump held too rosy a view of Putin’s desire to end the war, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had talked about the “horrific” loss of life in the nearly five-year war.
Trump envoy Steve Witkoff, who attended along with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, added: “He sent Jared and I here specifically to be a part of the Coalition of the Willing, and he’s given us instructions on doing everything possible to end this war and be supportive of that effort. And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with.”
One person who was in the room for the Trump call said the president talked in a general way, and made the point to leaders that a lot of people were dying in this war and countries should stop wasting money on it. Trump also told leaders that Putin is ready to have a negotiation to reach a peace deal, the same person said.
Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz said at the press conference, however, that Europe is providing funding for Ukrainian defense “to enable peace negotiations in the first place and to conduct them from a position of strength.”
Merz added: “We are not providing this strong support to prolong the war. We want to end this war.”
This is a developing story. Alex Gangitano contributed to this report from Washington. James Angelos contributed from Berlin.

Below is the unofficial transcript of CNBC's exclusive interview with Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei today, Thursday, November 19, following the company's highly anticipated IPO. Following are links to video on CNBC.com: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-ceo-on-scaling-laws-i-dont-think-we-really-believed-it-until-it-actually-happened.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropics-debut-is-one-stop-on-the-journey-says-daniela-amodei.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-weare-hoping-to-be-investment-grade-in-the-future.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-on-if-jensen-huang-should-come-back-as-ceo-.html , and https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-sibling-founders-reflect-on-ipo-journey.html .
All references must be sourced to CNBC.
ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Hey, thanks, Carl. Big day here. And I am here with the co-founders of this company, brother and sister. It's an unbelievable story, Dario and Daniela Amodei. Thank you for being here. Congratulations on this big moment.
DANIELA AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
DARIO AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
SORKIN: Here's where I want to start this. When I first met you, you basically just practically started the company. And I'm so curious — you understood scaling laws at the beginning, perhaps better than anybody, but did you ever expect three, four, five years later here we would be and be talking about evaluation that starts with a T?
DARIO AMODEI: You know, the funny thing is, you look at the scaling laws and they're a line on a piece of paper, right? They predict that a model will have certain cognitive capabilities that will be capable of certain economic tasks. But it's one thing to kind of draw that line, and it's a totally different thing to see the consequences out in the world. And so I would say the scaling laws kind of imply that the technology and hopefully our work within it would — would have this scale. But I don't think we really believed it until it actually happened.
SORKIN: And it's happening right now. Daniela, this is now going to be the largest public benefit corporation to go public. What — for those folks who are watching this morning, even thinking about investing in the company, what does that mean, both for the company itself, but also the way investors should think about that?
DANIELA AMODEI: So, as a public benefit corporation, you know, part of why we decided to incorporate this way, is Anthropic mission is so much about how do we build something that is good for everybody? How do we really build for the public benefit? And part of what I think is so interesting about this structure is that we're actually legally required to balance shareholder interest with the public benefit, with the public good. And I think when Dario and I and our other co-founders were starting the organization, you know, we learned about this concept of a public benefit corporation. It really spoke to us, because we said, well, that's exactly what we're trying to do. We're really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people.
SORKIN: OK, so here's the question. How do you balance the idea of growth and the idea of, for example, pacing at this point? This is something you have talked a lot about, pacing, given some of the safety concerns around AI? And how should the investor class think about those competing interests?
DARIO AMODEI: So, this, you know, this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company. But it's really, because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world, it's something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We're just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. And so, you think about something like pacing, the idea behind pacing was, you know, imagine that you have — you're driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour, right? This is models building themselves, recursive self-improvement. What we have done with pacing is essentially said, look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way. And you know, I think, in the long run, that will work out pretty well for the investors as well, because the company that builds the safest, that has trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that's going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company. And I think that's what we often look for. We look for synergies, ways to make the two line up in the long run.
SORKIN:  What does success look like today? When we see the price of this, do you say to yourself, if this is up 10 percent, 20 percent, that's success? If it's up too much, is that not success? What does, I mean, you guys have spent a lot of time with your bankers and—
DARIO AMODEI:  I think that's one of the very few topics we're not allowed to talk about.
DANIELA AMODEI:  I think, you know, I think maybe the way I would put it is, Anthropic has always been a very long-term-focused company, right? We have always been thinking about, how is this technology going to be beneficial to people in the future, but also what can it do for people today? And so while today is a super exciting milestone and we're obviously really, really excited about it, I think it's, for us, it's like one stop on the journey, right? We think about this as, wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic, for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company. And I think that's really, at least for me, what I have been focusing on today.
SORKIN:  The rate of growth of this company has been extraordinary, but I want to understand the unlock and also understand the competition in the space, because, increasingly, you have open-weight models. You have competitors in OpenAI, which are trying to offer tokens at cheaper prices. You have folks like Microsoft, which offer your services, and yet are also trying to sell their own models. And they say oftentimes that some of those models, or at least some of the features of their models, can do some of the same things, maybe not at the frontier level. How do you think about that in terms of what that means longer term to the margins for the company?
DARIO AMODEI:  So, I think, I think a couple concepts. One concept is the frontier. And we have found that there are these incredible returns to the frontier. And in most products or goods, you have competition on price. Here, the competition is really on quality, because the returns to greater cognitive ability are so high, right? As we climb the exponential of cognitive ability, you go from doing chatbots, to being able to do coding, to being able to do biology and robotics. And the economic value of things further along the frontier is so much larger than things earlier in the frontier that that's where most of the value accumulates. The second idea is that, if you're good at the frontier, you are also good at producing smaller and more efficient models away from the frontier. So, if you look at Haiku 5.5, we were able to drop the price by 4X from Haiku 4.5 and by many times from Opus and Fable 5 family, which are, which it's, which it's much cheaper than. And so we are able to also compete using our, the same technology that we build our models, models on the frontier, the same compute multipliers, to make these cheap models that compete away from the frontier.

articles.title_orig: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found Myanmar in breach of several of its obligations under international treaties to prevent and not to commit genocide .
The ICJ's president, Judge Yuji Iwasawa said that the panel of 15 judges had decided by nine votes to six that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine state .
The judges also found the country guilty of a series of other more specific violations by majority rulings.
"On the basis of all the evidence taken together, the Court is of the view that the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar's actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of... the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State," ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa said that Myanmar should make efforts to pay reparations to victims or their associates where possible and appropriate.
He also called for it to facilitate the safe return of refugees, and to take measures to investigate and, if necessary, prosecute individual wrongdoing by its nationals and security forces.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
The ICJ said in its consideration, the Rohingya constituted a distinct ethnic group with their own defining language and culture, as well as self-identifying as such. This means they qualified as a protected group for the purposes of international laws against genocide.
Myanmar's security forces "killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated acts of sexual violence, as well as extreme violence against children," and also attacked Rohingya as they tried to flee the fighting, the ICJ's Iwasawa said.
"The court is fully convinced that the 2017 clearance operations caused serious bodily and mental harm to a significant number of the protected group," Judge Iwasawa said.
Iwasawa also said that some civilian participation in the clearance operations could not necessarily be considered state-ordered or state-sanctioned behavior. But the court found that the government and security forces also made no meaningful efforts to prevent non-Rohingya civilian atrocities and fanned the flames of ethnic and religious tension.
At one point, reading the details of the findings, Iwasawa noted "Myanmar's failure, genuinely to investigate the alleged atrocities, and its refusal to facilitate access to evidence and witnesses, or provide information requested."
He said this meant it was possible the court did not have reliable knowledge of information available only from within Myanmar to which it was not given access.
There was no immediate response from the government in Myanmar or the military, which is regarded as the real underlying power.
Rohingya activist Yasmin Ullah — a Canadian citizen since 2016 but who was born in Rakhine state and who was a member of Gambia's delegation that filed the ICJ case — called the verdict more important for the world than for her community.
"The Rohingya never needed a court to tell us what happened to us," she said. "We needed the world to hear it, and today it has."
Wai Wai Nu, a Rohingya activist who directs the Women's Peace Network NGO, said the world's highest court's finding followed "decades" when "the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence and dismiss our suffering."
And the co-chair of the Arakan Rohingya National Council, Nay San Lwin, said that for Rohingya people, "justice means the restoration of our citizenship, recognition of our identity and our safe and dignified return home."
Myanmar's shadow national unity government, which includes remnants of former President Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy Party, said it "respects the authority" of the ICJ.
It said that since the beginning of the "revolution against military dictatorship" in 2021, it had affirmed its "commitment to the rule of law, human rights, justice and states' obligations to prevent and punish genocide."
Myanmar was under nominally civilian rule at the time of the atrocities, but the extent to which Suu Kyi's government held sway over the military and its actions is debatable.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres welcomed Thursday's verdict, calling it a "powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide" and noting it was the first verdict of its kind against a state.
"Myanmar must act in accordance with its obligation to comply with the Court's decision," Guterres said in a statement, adding that this includes "the safe, voluntary and dignified return [of Rohingya] to their place of residence nad reunification of families."
Gambia's Justice Minister Dawda Jallow, who attended the hearing, spoke to reporters afterward at the Peace Palace in The Hague.
"The victory belongs to the Rohingya," Jallow said. "They survived. They testified. And today, they will believe."
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband issued a statement saying the former colonial power was "taking immediate action today in light of this judgment."
Miliband said Britain would expel Myanmar's defense attache in London and was calling for a special UN Security Council session in response. He called on Myanmar to "comply fully with the judgment," and on the international community to "play its part in supporting implementation, accountability, and justice for the Rohingya."
UN human rights chief Volker Türk said the ruling "clearly concludes the State of Myanmar stands responsible for one of the most egregious crimes known to humankind."
The case centers around the military crackdown in Rakhine state on the country's western coastline against the predominantly Muslim Rohingya minority in 2017.
Violence had been brewing for several years beforehand, but the most intense phase of the military crackdown in the north of region was triggered by a coordinated attack by a Muslim militia group against several police and military installations and personnel in August 2017.
A UN fact finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the military clearance operations that followed. Around 700,000 people fled to Bangladesh, where most still reside in the world's largest refugee camp .
Gambia filed the complaint at The Hague in 2019, alleging a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder designed to wipe out the Rohingya minority in whole or in part.
Myanmar's influential military, now back in full de facto control of the country albeit amid a long-running civil war, has maintained that it was engaged in a legitimate counterinsurgency.
Aung San Suu Kyi , who was the civilian president at the time, took a slightly more nuanced stance, but nevertheless traveled to The Hague to contest the charges, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."
The case is likely to draw close attention from those pursuing ICJ prosecutions against Israel and Benjamin Netanyahu for the war in Gaza and against Russia and Vladimir Putin for the invasion of Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.title_zh: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.content_orig:
Concerns about balance sheets and valuations in the artificial intelligence sector have hit the market hard since October, and investors who have shorted publicly traded tech companies in the AI trade have profited. Most investors don't think as much about "shorting" debt, but there will be a way through exchange-traded funds to profit from widening credit default swap spreads of top AI companies.
Both Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs have filed for funds that target the credit default swaps of companies closely linked to the AI trade, from CoreWeave and Oracle to the Magnificent Seven: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft Corporation, Nvidia, Tesla, and Apple.
Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. CDS is a closely watched indicator of issuer health in the debt markets, especially in the AI market this year. The ETFs are designed to gain when the CDS spreads of these companies widen, either as a group in the case of a Magnificent Seven CDS fund, or individually in the case of proposed ETFs targeting Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta. The funds would lose value when the market assesses the creditworthiness of these debt issuers as improving.
Both ETF managers filed for CoreWeave and Oracle CDS funds, specifically, among broader AI and semiconductor company CDS portfolios.
If the exchange-traded fund managers get approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission, these portfolios would be the first of their kind in an ETF market that has become more aggressive in recent years about launching higher-risk strategies revolving around more complex financial instruments than just public stocks and bonds. The ETF managers plan to employ leverage in the portfolios, which both increases risk and the potential for outsized returns on any given day, similar to the way existing single-stock leverage and inverse ETFs function.
The ETF managers say these CDS funds can serve an important role in a market on edge about AI debt.
"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates and companies take on significant capital commitments to fund that growth, we see an opportunity to give investors more targeted tools to manage credit risk and hedge potential financial stress across some of the biggest names driving the AI buildout," Sylvia Jablonski, CIO of Defiance ETFs, said in a statement to CNBC.
Neocloud companies like CoreWeave are a major focus for AI skeptics, an AI bubble watch compounded by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia, who is seen as a critical player in financing the AI buildout, with Nvidia called by some the "central bank of AI ."
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan on Tuesday said that neocloud company AI projects could face an existential crisis if Nvidia funding dries up. "There was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground," Rowan said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ." "If that banking function, that guarantor function, gets taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear."
In its earnings filings and conference call on Tuesday, Nvidia shifted the tone in discussing the way it finances the AI ecosystem.
Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said it is less likely that these ETFs will find an audience among retail investors than smaller institutional players.
"It may be a stretch for the average retail guy," he said, but he added that having managed leveraged and inverse ETFs, it is clear that many investors "get interested" when a particular asset is seeing outsized moves, as has been the case with AI company-linked CDS in 2026. "The stuff that moves a lot is the stuff that tends to generate the most interest," he said.
Both prospectuses stress that these funds are not designed to move inversely to the reference companies' stocks and can lose money while a company's shares decline. They also note these funds don't short bonds or bet directly against a company's stock, and to buy CDS protection, they pay premiums, which are a unique cost to the fund manager whether or not credit conditions worsen.
The CDS of these companies have been on the move in a major way as part of the AI trade over the past year.
CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 is yielding close to 16%, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps were recently between 1,100-1,200. Spreads over 1,000 are generally considered a sign of distress.
CoreWeave executives have taken their messaging about the debt public, with co-founder and chief strategy officer Brian Venturo posting on X.com on Wednesday that he had purchased $30 million in unsecured company bonds and was going to hold them until maturity in 2031. "I've never been more confident in CoreWeave," he wrote.
Oracle CDS contracts have moved up over the past year from below 80 to a current range above 300.
The CDS spreads on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon and Meta as examples, rose over 100% within the past year, as their free cash flow turned negative from spending heavily on AI. Even though the market is much less concerned about their balance sheets than that of the neoclouds, major tech company CDS spreads did hit five-year highs earlier this month.
Tuttle said that these ETFs, if approved, would be the "easiest" to use for smaller institutions and family offices that want CDS exposure and "are either too small to trade with the Goldmans of the world or lack the in-house expertise to trade CDS on their own."
"It is a different way to hedge the AI trade," Tuttle said.
ETF investing experts expressed skepticism about this approach and market reception. "I don't see much demand materializing for these types of products," said Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management. But he added it does make sense to target these ETFs "at retail investors who are seeing scary headlines around AI capex spending. Yet another way to speculate (gamble)," he said.
Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said he foresees confusion with how these funds will work. "How many non-professionals know what CDS are?" he said.
Tuttle says it won't take billions in assets to make an ETF focused on AI CDS a minor financial success. "My criteria is I want to see a runway to $20 million, which is about our breakeven. I see it here. It doesn't mean it will happen, but I think we have a decent chance."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report

articles.content_orig:
It comes as several companies have reported technology issues in recent days.
A pair of technology failures at Apple and Marriott International follow several other recent major outages at the FAA, United Airlines and Microsoft, highlighting the risks of depending on one of just a few major providers of essential technology.
The outages are just the latest in a string of technology breakdowns in recent days.
JPMorgan Chase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went to Capitol Hill on Wednesday to talk about worldwide threats since Sept. 11, 2001, but he was in the hot seat over questions about technology issues that disrupted millions of Americans over the last week.
Mullin testified before the House Committee on Homeland Security for a hearing underway titled "Worldwide Threats to the Homeland: 25 Years After 9/11" along with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia.
Mullin, Clayton and Raia were also questioned about the cyber outages that have affected airlines, Microsoft Outlook, banks and other services.
In his opening remarks, Clayton reaffirmed that recent cyber incidents causing disruptions for multiple companies and networks do not appear to be the result of coordinated cyberattacks — despite widespread speculation among the public.

Marriott said Wednesday that a technical issue that affected sign-in capabilities on Marriott.com and the Marriott Bonvoy app has been resolved.
"Our review found no indication that the disruption was cybersecurity-related, and we appreciate our guests' patience as we worked to address the issue," the company said in a statement.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Tuesday sought to assure Americans that there's 'zero' information that a series of outages and technical failures across the US are related to each other or to a malign actor.
Rubio looked to calm Americans as he was traveling with President Donald Trump as they prepared to leave Manila for key meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China.
"We have zero evidence or any reason to believe that any of these isolated or individual instances have anything to do with nefarious actors, with cyber hackers, with criminals, with another nation state, with a malign actor of any kind," Rubio said.

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global powerbroker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. He made an appeal for regional harmony, saying: “Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.”
However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the US president calling the Russian his “friend”. The peace declaration said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Sanofi weighs takeover of US drugmaker Insmed, Bloomberg News reports
articles.title_zh: Sanofi weighs takeover of US drugmaker Insmed, Bloomberg News reports
articles.content_orig:
After Sanofi leadership telegraphed an upsized appetite for business development last month, signals have emerged that the French Pharma may be eyeing a deal to acquire Insmed, the developer of new respiratory medicine Brinsupri, which appears well on its way to cementing its blockbuster status this year.
Sanofi is now speaking with advisers as it appraises a potential acquisition of Insmed, Bloomberg first reported Thursday, citing confidential sources close to the matter. Under recently arrived CEO Belén Garijo, M.D., Ph.D., Sanofi has been assessing the levers it can pull as it looks to mount a defense against a looming Dupixent patent cliff and a series of recent pipeline misfires.
But the talks over a possible Insmed buyout are ongoing and it could still be weeks before a deal emerges, if at all, Bloomberg’s sources stressed. Sanofi could eventually forego making an offer, and other bidders may step up to the plate too, they added.
Spokespeople at both Sanofi and Insmed declined to comment on the report when reached by Fierce.
Speaking to journalists during the company’s third-quarter earnings call in October, financial chief François-Xavier Roger told Fierce that Sanofi will pursue external growth opportunities as it attempts to straighten out its near-term trajectory. He signaled “an increased interest in late-stage and commercial medicines in our core disease areas, complemented with disciplined built-in acquisitions of early-stage projects.”
Adding that those business development and M&A opportunities could carry a higher price tag than Sanofi had originally planned for, Roger said that the company aimed to share more on its priorities by year-end, while cautioning against the likelihood of a major transaction over the next couple months.
Beyond near-term potential revenue drivers, which an Insmed deal could deliver—and in familiar respiratory territory for Sanofi—the company is also appraising “what we call white spaces or moonshots with unmet medical needs,” Roger said last month in reference to his company’s broader external priorities.
From its protective antibody for RSV, Beyfortus, to flu shots and COVID vaccines, plus its immunology stalwart Dupixent, Sanofi would be well positioned to leverage its existing respiratory expertise around Brinsupri.
Approved last summer, Insmed’s Brinsupri became the first DPP1 inhibitor to hit the U.S. market after clearance from the FDA to treat non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFBE) in adults and kids ages 12 years and older. At the time of approval, analysts at Mizuho predicted Brinsupri could eventually lock up $6.6 billion in peak sales in that indication alone.
NCFBE causes the walls of the body’s airways to widen and thicken from inflammation and infection. This primarily leads to frequent coughing as the body tries to clear infected mucus.
Insmed itself has pinned high hopes on Brinsupri’s sales trajectory, with CEO Will Lewis calling his company’s 2026 sales forecast of $1 billion “audacious” when it was first revealed earlier this year. At the time, Lewis noted that the Brinsupri launch had “surpassed even our most ambitious expectations,” which he said were informed by a “basket of historically strong respiratory launches.”
Insmed reported a little over $917 million in global Brinsupri sales over the first nine months of 2026. The company now expects total sales of the drug to hit $1.35 billion to $1.4 billion this year.
Still, the road for Brinsupri hasn’t been entirely without potholes.
Back in March, Insmed called it quits on a program studying the drug in adults with moderate to severe hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) after a phase 2b trial failed to hit its primary or secondary endpoints. And a few months before that in December, Insmed ended its Brinsupri efforts in chronic rhinosinusitis without nasal polyps (CRSsNP).
Insmed also boasts another commercial product in Arikayce, a nebulizer-based treatment for mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease that was approved in 2018.
Insmed’s stock price was up more than 18% as of early afternoon Thursday.
With a current potential value now exceeding $30 billion, a buyout of Insmed could mark one of the biggest for the pharma industry since Pfizer’s mammoth $43 billion offer for Seagen back in 2023.
While holding off on commentary as to the report's validity, the team of Matt Phipps, Ph.D., at William Blair wrote Thursday that Sanofi is seen as a "rational fit" as a possible Insmed buyer, highlighting the respiratory overlap.
The biggest questions then, in the analysts' estimation, are whether Sanofi has capacity for the deal, and the price at which Insmed would be comfortable selling. It remains to be seen if Sanofi, with some 12 billion euros in current net debt, could "truly afford" an acquisition approaching $40 billion, Phipps' team said.
Still, investors have also speculated that Sanofi could add some Insmed assets to its joint venture with Regeneron to afford additional capital flexibility, if a deal truly is in the offing, the analysts pointed out.

articles.title_orig: 'Come to Moscow,' Putin urges Europeans after Shenzhen summit
articles.title_zh: 'Come to Moscow,' Putin urges Europeans after Shenzhen summit
articles.content_orig:
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.
The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.
Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.
"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.
It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other European leaders about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."
"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X .
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA VI’ Beats ‘The Odyssey’ Revenue On Release Day, Estimate Says
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA VI’ Beats ‘The Odyssey’ Revenue On Release Day, Estimate Says
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI is here at last and gamers around the world can finally play after it launched at midnight globally. So far the game, which takes up a whopping 212GB on your PlayStation5 or Xbox , is receiving rave reviews . GTA 6 is streaming all over Twitch and the memes, clips and hot takes are pouring in.
Digital marketing firm Sensor Tower estimates that GTA 6 pre-orders have already topped $1.65 billion in sales. GTA 6 costs $79.99 for PS5 and Xbox , with an "ultimate" version priced at $99.99.
Players began pre-loading GTA 6 last week, even though they probably had to clear some space on their consoles. Millions of people are expected to take time off work and school to play GTA 6 . Xbox has a doctor's note from DJ Khaled (aka Dr. Xbox) that may be the excuse you need (but you'll probably want to clear it with your boss either way).
PlayStation's network suffered a brief outage Wednesday afternoon as the game became available and players made the required update to their consoles. But since Wednesday evening, it's been smooth sailing.
Here's what people are saying about GTA VI today:
Leonida has plenty of adorable animals roaming around, but there's one that has captured the attention of the entire internet: jet ski dog. You can find the dog driving his very own jet ski around the waters of Leonida, proving it's a pretty capable pup.
Rockstar might have had some real-life inspiration for the sea-bound buddy, too. There's reportedly a dog named Loosy who is known in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, for riding a jet ski around the area. Cute!
We've already seen plenty of celebrities and singers featured as the voice actors for characters and radio DJs in GTA 6 , but we now have confirmation of the first star athlete in the game. Miami Dolphins wide receiver Tyreek Hill is the inspiration for Maleek Rivers, a football star who plays for the Vice City Manatees in the game.
GTA 6 received quite a bit of attention ahead of its release after Rockstar revealed some of the celebrities it tapped to be radio hosts for the in-game stations, including big names like Lana Del Rey and Bad Bunny. Now that the game is out, we're discovering even more celebrities and musicians that were kept a secret. Here's a look at some of the others that have been confirmed so far:
Charlamagne tha God and Ivy Rivera on Early AF Radio
Antonio Carbonaro and Seth Troxler on Circoloco Records
PinkPantheress and the Dare on Stockyard FM
Earlier today, we also learned that parody legend "Weird" Al Yankovic hosts the game's '80s hits station, Vice City FM.
We're sure more celebrity cameos will be found as people dig deeper into the game, but it's been a pretty stacked cast so far.
With 13 years between GTA 5 and GTA 6 , Rockstar had a lot of time to polish the game world and pack it with plenty of detail that has left both reviewers and players stunned . But all that detail takes a toll when the action gets going. The game targets 30 frames per second (FPS) for normal gameplay, but some players have reported it dropping to 15 to 20 FPS during fights on the base PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series S consoles.
If you're not a gamer, FPS essentially determines how "smooth" a game feels and describes how many individual frames of gameplay are shown every second. Many gamers view 30 FPS as the floor for smooth gameplay, and 60 FPS or higher as the gold standard. Once you start dropping below 30, gameplay can feel choppy and laggy.
The top-end Xbox Series X and PlayStation 5 Pro appear to have an easier time sticking close to that 30 FPS mark due to their more powerful hardware. If you're interested in a technical breakdown, you can check out Digital Foundry's excellent GTA 6 tech review .
One beloved GTA 6 meme may be heading off into retirement with the new game's launch, but it has already birthed a hilarious new one. X user @MurdoinkGS added a green screen to the in-game phone screen in a clip of a player mindlessly running over beachgoers in a vehicle. The internet understood the assignment, replacing the green screen effect with all kinds of distracting content, ranging from a Hasan Piker Twitch stream to Pokémon Go and more.
It hasn't totally broken the internet so far, but the launch of GTA 6 helped set a new internet usage record , according to Frankfurt, Germany-based internet exchange operator DE-CIX.
Wednesday night, data throughput across DE-CIX's internet exchanges worldwide reached a new high of 33.03 TB per second. Data transfer and usage during the midnight launch of GTA 6 was 25% higher than usual, the company said.
Data traffic also spiked about 20% after the GTA 6 download period opened on Nov. 10, DE-CIX said, with roughly 13 downloads of the game every second in Germany.
If you're getting up to some nefarious stuff in GTA 6 , you might want to watch your back. Players have found Dexter Morgan's apartment and boat from the Showtime series Dexter in the game. We haven't seen any signs that the Florida-based serial killer himself is in the game, but you can find his "toolkit" on the roof of his apartment building — complete with a syringe for incapacitating his targets.
One of the GTA series' biggest strengths is its penchant for pop-culture satire and references, so it isn't surprising to see there's a Dexter reference in Leonida — a fictional Florida. We're sure players will be discovering pop-culture references throughout the game for a long, long time to come.
When the release date for Grand Theft Auto VI was announced earlier this year, U.S. Army soldiers at Fort Stewart, Georgia, were given the opportunity to sign up for a four-day weekend off to play the game — if they re-enlisted for two years of additional military service.
According to Task & Purpose , a website focused on the U.S. military community, 43 soldiers in the 9th Brigade Engineer Battalion took the offer.
An Army spokesperson told the site that most participants "already had reasons to remain in the military" and described the gaming offer as "an added bonus rather than necessarily the deciding factor."
A Singaporean couple who drew up an agreement with "rules" for playing GTA 6 once it launched said it was meant as a joke. But Julian Tay and Lisa Chan told CNN that a lot of the online reaction showed people may have missed the point (which is not exactly a first on the internet).
The agreement, which runs from launch day, Nov. 19, through Nov. 29 allows Tay to play as much as he wants over that time, with questions and requests on hold until an in-game mission ends. Any hugs or errands have to wait for a break in between missions, and dismissive comments from Chan if Tay fails a mission aren't allowed. It also stipulates that everything that happens in game is fictional.
When they posted a video of the contract last month, the couple heard some immediate feedback from many online who thought the contract raised red flags.
"There was quite a lot of backlash when we made the video, and everyone was like, 'Oh, leave him,'" Tay told CNN .
But Chan said it was always intended to be tongue-in-cheek, theorizing people were maybe projecting some insecurities about their own relationships onto them. She told CNN she plans to watch him play the game, and even put together a GTA-themed care package for him.
One of the biggest benefits of taking 13 years to release a game? Rockstar had plenty of time to make the map absolutely massive. Now, the map has been fully revealed, showing just how large Leonida is. One streamer, who goes by AngelMelly online, said she spent eight hours fully revealing the map in-game.
Considering the amount of detail on the map, ranging from the bustling Vice City to swamplands and beaches, it looks like GTA 6 players will have enough to sink their teeth into for a long time.

articles.title_orig: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
articles.title_zh: AI's great divergence: Machines accelerate as makers unravel
articles.content_orig:
The logo of Anthropic is visible on a laptop screen against a Nasdaq-100 candlestick chart. The company is scheduled to begin trading on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Silas Stein/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)
In 1965, Irving John Good, a mathematician who worked alongside Alan Turing, proposed the concept of the “ ultraintelligent ” machine. “Let an ultraintelligent machine be defined as a machine that can far surpass all the intellectual activities of any man, however clever. Since the design of machines is one of these intellectual activities, an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines; there would then unquestionably be an ‘intelligence explosion,’ and the intelligence of man would be left far behind,” he wrote.
Today, the prospect of an “intelligence explosion” is attached to another speculative concept in the field of artificial intelligence, recursive self-improvement (RSI). This term is tied to the increasing capacity for AI systems to produce code without human supervision.
In May, Anthropic claimed that its large language model, Claude, had written 80% of the company’s merged code . METR, an independent organization with close ties to the industry it monitors, recently published a report commissioned by Anthropic. The report estimated that Anthropic’s benchmark scores improved last year at a rate that would have taken two years in the years before, and claimed (“with substantial uncertainty,” they note) that 80% of the acceleration is due to AI assistance in code development. METR reports that the most useful evidence it observed to arrive at this estimate was redacted by Anthropic, since supposedly it might help other companies develop similar techniques. Anthropic is slated to launch its initial public offering, aiming for a valuation of $1.4 trillion, on Nov. 18.
The “intelligence explosion” is one of the promises of the AI boom, and “boom” is the key word here: Eliezer Yudkowsky, who popularized the term RSI, suggests that a “seed AI” system would serve as a catalyst to an explosive powder keg of exponential capabilities. As the phrase implies, once the system can improve, it can beget an improved version of itself, and so on. This belief in recursion, paired with METR’s report, has led influential AI observers to expect accelerated timelines for RSI. For example, Dwarkesh Patel predicted last week that the world is “a couple of months away ... from AIs that are as good as the best humans at AI research,” and that this, in turn, will lead to AI that is “at least as good the best human experts in every field” by 2030, or earlier.
The reality is likely more complicated. Many of the measures in the METR report were based on specific benchmarks, which can limit the kind of problems that can be assessed to the kinds of problems that can be included on a test . Additionally, METR does not report on the kinds of tests that were evaluated. But a hallmark of these assessments is that the answers are automatically verifiable: they can be checked as true or false, right or wrong, following an automatable logic.
The increase in such capacities is specifically trained into the models through Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), a sleeper innovation that accounts for a number of capacity improvements in the past year, particularly in coding and math. RLVR has accounted for what many users experienced as a shift in capability in early 2025 as it was integrated well across a number of systems. RLVR is a form of post-training that optimizes models to do precisely the kind of writing that results in verifiable answers.
RLVR takes a base model and measures the text it produces to fetch a verifiable answer, like those on the tests. When the model succeeds, the text it produces is understood as a desirable pattern, and steps are taken to ensure more of that kind of text is produced in the next stage of training. This produces longer text that expands the likelihood of correct answers, but also emphasizes particular tokens and language that can cause the model to rewrite text from different frames.
RLVR explains these capabilities rather than diminishing them, and code — the topic at the heart of the RSI push — is a verifiable task. But if the models are showing stronger capacities for these kinds of tasks, it does not follow that the models are advancing in other ways needed to facilitate their own exponential improvement.
A fully enclosed, self-perpetuating recursive system, without a capacity for redirection, becomes a feedback loop akin to the sound leaving a speaker and entering the same system through a microphone, creating echoes that break apart into a wall of horrid sound. That sound you’re hearing may not be the sonic boom of AI growth hitting the speed barrier, but a breakdown in how the system selects tasks: they converge.
You have successfully joined our subscriber list.
AI agents currently operate as multiple instances running on the same training. For recursive amplification to work, you need diversity in the input. It’s not an impossible task, but it’s a strikingly different setup from setting a stochastic flock (or “agentic swarm”) loose on a series of tasks that can be automatically graded.
An important question to ask, then, is what, precisely, is the “self” in recursive self-improvement? A recent technical paper suggests that “every improvement loop is a claim that some signal can substitute for human judgment.” Self-improvement is tied to the quality of a specific automated replacement installed for a specific automated task. How we draw the boundaries around a system can help us understand what it is able to do. Automate variety well, and you can create better systems. But something has to generate a signal, and something has to change that signal. Right now, a model cannot generate signals of the same quality across different layers of its own architecture.
A research paper from this summer articulates the consequences of these limits well. The question of the paper was whether AI agents could conduct AI research . The authors gave models research questions from papers written by human researchers that had been submitted to NeurIPS 2026 but not yet published. They asked the models to tackle the same research question, without access to those papers, and then had the human researchers grade the agents on the research. The models were left to scaffold an experimental design that could answer the question, execute it and evaluate the results.
Beyond engineering the scaffolding, the models failed spectacularly. They did not take feedback and did not recalibrate when paths became obviously fruitless, supporting the hypothesis that “[a]gents can’t hill-climb their way into choosing a set of candidate hypotheses, deciding what evidence would settle a research question, or incorporating feedback effectively and recognizing that an approach has failed and the right move is to start over,” as the authors wrote. Left unattended, the machines kept repeating themselves into a microphone, rather than trying to find a new source of information or shift to a new set of ideas.
It could be tempting for advocates who want to believe that RSI is around the corner to dismiss this as a failure of existing models when nobody has suggested RSI is in these models. I take the experiment as a measure of the gaps between signals of strength and weakness. Machines can become better at narrow tasks that benchmarks excel at capturing, but the same models consistently fall apart in an open world of vast possibilities.
Prediction is a fool’s game, and even as a critical observer of large language models and image models I am continually surprised by them. But I am unconvinced when I hear predictions of future capacities based on following trendlines unrelated to the capacities being promised. Benchmarks are a particularly challenging trajectory to rely upon, as they are easily gamified, and often test for precise forms of p
