articles.title_orig: Palmer Luckey at DealBook: 'China wants Jensen out, so I want him in', and Musk shouldn't have to risk Starlink for Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Palmer Luckey at DealBook: 'China wants Jensen out, so I want him in', and Musk shouldn't have to risk Starlink for Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk believes he’s helped Ukraine stay alive in the war, claiming Russia would have steamrolled the country if SpaceX hadn’t supplied Kyiv with its crucial Starlink satellite internet.
The billionaire tech tycoon touted himself as Kyiv’s ultimate private-sector savior, boasting that his Starlink tech gave Ukrainian forces a fighting chance, in a Thursday interview with CNBC .
“I think it would probably be accurate to say that there is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have,” Musk boasted . “I made sure that Starlink was in Ukraine prepositioned ahead of the Russian invasion.”
Musk insisted that Starlink stood as Ukraine’s sole indestructible line of defense when Russian strongman Vladimir Putin sent his troops in.
“And when Russia invaded, they disabled all communications, all cell towers, all fiber cables, and every satellite communication system,” he added.
“There was one system they could not disable, and that was Starlink.”
The SpaceX chief insisted that his telecommunications network remains the only thing holding the war-torn country together.
“If we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately,” he claimed.
Ukrainian officials cried foul last month over their access to Starlink , when they discovered issues with it involving their drones traveling at speeds of 160 km/h or more. Russian drones at the time were traveling at 400 km/h or higher.
The situation occurred shortly after President Trump announced a controversial diesel deal with Putin.
The billionaire claimed Ukraine had been using the civilian “Net system, Starlink, to carry out drone attacks against Russia” and said SpaceX took action to stop that.
If the Ukrainian military wants to use Starlink for defense operations, Musk said they must work directly through the US government to acquire “Star Shield.”
“It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people,” he cautioned.
“If you want to do that, you need to do Star Shield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government.”
Musk also maintained he won’t be made responsible for battlefield carnage.
“SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR,” he said defiantly on X .
“That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict.”

articles.title_orig: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews after 13-year wait
articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI launches to rave reviews after 13-year wait
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto VI has launched to rave reviews, in one of the most hotly anticipated releases in gaming history.
Gamers got their hands on the latest instalment of the GTA franchise on Thursday, as critics hailed the open-world game as a “masterpiece”, “spectacular”, and an “astonishing American epic”.
The immersive game had an aggregate score of 99 out of 100 on Metacritic, based on more than 150 reviews, as it began dropping on game consoles worldwide from midnight.
“Exquisitely detailed, endlessly ripe for experimentation, and uncompromisingly engineered, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the single most impressive video game I have ever played,” critic Luke Reilly wrote in a gushing review for gaming website IGN.
“Accepting that GTA 6 is very much not real also makes it all the more astonishing how much the game is very real,” reviewer Jordan Minor wrote in PCMag.
Grand Theft Auto VI follows the exploits of Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos, a Bonnie and Clyde-like duo who become entangled in a criminal conspiracy after a seemingly easy score goes awry.
Players have free rein to explore the hyper-realistic fictional state of Leonida and its coastal metropolis of Vice City, stand-ins for Florida and Miami.
Like previous entries in the series, Grand Theft Auto VI features graphic depictions of crime and violence, with players able to mow down pedestrians in stolen vehicles and engage in shootouts with police.
The game, developed by New York-based Rockstar Games at an estimated cost of more than $1bn, is the first instalment in the series since the release of Grand Theft Auto V in 2013.
Originally set to go on sale in 2025, the release was delayed twice to allow developers to polish up gameplay.
Grand Theft Auto VI, which is available on the PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series, is likely to be the most lucrative release in the history of the gaming industry, which is projected to be worth as much as $350bn by the end of the decade.
Pre-orders for Grand Theft Auto VI exceeded an estimated 15.8 million units as of November 17, generating $1.54bn in revenue, according to the market intelligence platform Sensor Tower.
The GTA series began in 1997 with the launch of Grand Theft Auto, a 2D top-down open-world game available on the personal computer, PlayStation and Game Boy Color.

articles.title_orig: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
articles.title_zh: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
articles.content_orig:
MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.
The automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck , which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.
The production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.
The automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.
Alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as quickly as possible.
"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells."
The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
In September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.
Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.
Ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the company's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.
Ford has said the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.
The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it plans to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

articles.title_orig: Walmart is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.title_zh: Walmart is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.content_orig:
Walmart is scheduled to report its third fiscal quarter earnings Thursday as the retailer prepares for the holiday season with an increased emphasis on value amid lower consumer sentiment.
The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.
Here's what the company is expected to report for its fiscal third quarter, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Walmart previously said it expects third-quarter net sales to climb 3% to 3.75%. CFO John David Rainey told CNBC last quarter that Walmart's "business is strong" and that he's encouraged by its progress.
The company is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef. It also saw a significant boost from tariff refunds, which Rainey said Walmart would use to cut prices.
In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with its club subsidiary, Sam's Club, as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer standalone memberships.
The retailer is also rolling out technology in its stores to improve the customer experience, including light-up digital shelf labels that are connected to its app. Those shelf labels and Walmart's AI push have also sparked concerns that the retailer could try to change prices based on demand and shoppers' personal data, which Walmart has denied.
Analysts from UBS wrote in a note last week that they believe the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results will show healthy market share gains.
"E-commerce continues to scale, the company's higher-margin alternative revenue streams continue to grow and Walmart is increasingly able to fund investments in price and convenience while still producing attractive operating income growth," the analysts wrote.
They added that they expect Walmart's fourth-quarter outlook to include "robust operating income growth."
Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year-to-date.

articles.title_zh: DealBook Summit: Elon Musk Paints Himself as Political Moderate, Says He Is ‘Not MAGA’
articles.content_orig:
By continuing to use our site, you agree to our Privacy Policy and Terms of Use .
Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images
The billionaire’s comments came during an interview at the New York Times DealBook summit.
Elon Musk, who spent nearly half a billion dollars on Republican campaigns in the recent U.S. midterm elections, is now claiming he is “not MAGA” after a historic blue wave secured Democratic majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.
“I’m not MAGA,” the Tesla and SpaceX CEO told attendees of the New York Times DealBook summit on Wednesday in a video interview with journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin.
The remark came after Sorkin pressed Musk, speaking remotely from the AMEC Summit in China, over public comments and posts he has made about the issue of immigration. A July Guardian analysis found that the near-trillionaire made twice as many X posts on the subject race and immigration ahead of SpaceX’s initial public offering than he did about his company.
“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he continued. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
The claim marks an about-face for a man who has campaigned with President Donald Trump, worn MAGA hats, and openly called himself “dark gothic MAGA.” Musk was not just the largest individual donor in the 2026 election cycle but across all of U.S. history, according to the Washington Post .
Throughout the conversation, Musk attempted to paint himself as having a more moderate political agenda, saying that he believes D.C. trifectas are dangerous, and claiming that his actual goal was securing a narrow Republican majority in the Senate.
“I think I’m ideologically quite moderate,” he said, adding, “I don’t think I have any kind of extreme political views.”
Elsewhere in the interview, Musk expressed buyer’s remorse over his massive political spending in the 2026 cycle, saying, “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it.”
“Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he added.
Musk’s $446 million spending in the 2026 cycle came atop more than $240 million spent on Republican campaigns in the 2024 presidential election. In both cycles, GOP advertising frequently deployed anti-LGBTQ+ and specifically anti-transgender rhetoric in an attempt to turn out voters. That strategy proved far more successful electorally in 2024 than it did in 2026. Overall, Republicans spent an estimated $183 million on anti-trans advertising in the midterms ahead of widespread losses.
As the New York Times reported, Musk’s America PAC specifically focused in September on the issue of trans participation in sports to try to defeat Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, and Josh Turek, who were campaigning in Texas, Ohio, and Iowa, respectively. Talarico, Brown, and Turek all won their races.

articles.title_orig: Was China Sending a Musical Message to Japan’s Takaichi During APEC Welcome?
articles.title_zh: Was China Sending a Musical Message to Japan’s Takaichi During APEC Welcome?
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title_orig: APEC live: Trump says US has been 'Pacific power for hundreds of years'
articles.title_zh: APEC live: Trump says US has been 'Pacific power for hundreds of years'
articles.content_orig:
Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. © Reuters
SHENZHEN -- Chinese President Xi Jinping is hosting leaders including U.S. counterpart Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin at this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, showcasing his own country's technological prowess against a backdrop of cold and hot conflicts.
The proceedings in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen kicked off with a CEO Summit of business leaders on Tuesday, to be followed by an Economic Leaders' Meeting beginning Wednesday. On the sidelines, Xi and Trump are expected to have their third summit of the year as they seek to manage a fraught superpower rivalry.
As the Ukraine war drags on and tensions with Iran simmer, all eyes are on a trilateral summit among Xi, Trump and Putin that the White House has said will happen on Thursday. This prospect has drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference among the U.S., U.K. and Soviet Union to discuss the fate of postwar Europe in 1945.
Before departing for Asia on Monday, Trump told reporters that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, a surprise announcement that could become another focal point of his visit.
Nikkei Asia is on the ground in Shenzhen to cover the meetings.

Here are the latest developments (Shenzhen time):
2:57 p.m. The Trump-Xi bilateral summit has ended, CCTV says.
2:49 p.m. Meanwhile, Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, and then exited to its northeast.
2:10 p.m. The Kremlin said the issue of Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral, Reuters reported, citing Russia's Tass news agency.
Trump had said that he plans discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi, and later with Xi and Putin in the bilateral.
2:06 p.m. Xi described China-U.S. relations as overall stable and improving and added he was willing to work with Trump to continue steering bilateral ties on the correct course.
"I remain committed to working with you," Xi said to Trump.
Trump also said he planned to discuss ending Ukraine war with Xi and Putin in the trilateral.
1:58 p.m. Trump said at the start of his bilateral meeting with Xi that the U.S.-China Board of Trade has brought balance to the relationship between the two countries and that they have split up tariffs in fair ways.
Trump added that he and Xi felt strongly that oil should flow through the Strait of Hormuz, where an Iranian blockade in response to U.S.-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic has restricted shipments and pushed up energy prices. The U.S. president said he will ask China to do more for American farmers, staunch supporters of the Republican party.
1:40 p.m. Trump and Xi pose in front of U.S. and Chinese flags for photos
1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.
12:43 p.m. Trump met with Putin on the sidelines of the APEC forum following the plenary leaders session. Their meeting comes ahead a bilateral between Trump and Xi and a trilateral among the three leaders.
"We've had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they'll come out of this," Trump told Putin.
1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.
12:35 p.m. Elon Musk told an APEC organizer that he was a "super fan" of China, according to a social media post by Yuyuan Tiantian, an account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
According to the post, the Tesla and SpaceX boss told Ren Hongbin, president of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, about his admiration for China's "magnificent buildings and natural landscapes" as well as its railway system.
Tesla will continue to increase production in China, Musk said, according to the post. He was photographed sitting in a room across Ren, wearing a black jacket, pants and shoes.
12:06 p.m. APEC plenary session ends
10:58 a.m. Putin tells his APEC counterparts that Russia contributes to regional energy security and that they can "always count on Moscow." He also invites all regional partners to use Russian logistics infrastructure.
10:39 a.m. Trump spoke about the U.S. economy and claimed his administration is taming inflation. He also said in his remarks that trade deals were forthcoming.
"The United States has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, and we continue to work to promote growth and stability, sovereignty, prosperity, and peace throughout this region," he said.
Trump also said AI regulation needed to be carefully managed and opposed measures that would "stifle" the industry. "We won't allow that to happen," he said.
Trump said he looked forward to meeting with Xi and Putin later this afternoon. but did not elaborate. The trilateral will follow a two-way meeting between Xi and Trump, their third this year.
10:30 a.m. Putin is taking the opportunity presented by APEC to shore up ties with Asian partners. He and Vietnamese leader To Lam agreed to step up cooperation with "a focus on traditional and new energy, including nuclear power, wind power and gas-fired power," according to Vietnam's readout.
The statement also says they "underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security and stability, increasing dialogue and cooperation, and upholding the role of multilateralism, the United Nations and the fundamental principles of international law."
10:10 a.m. In his opening address, Xi called for cooperation on Al and supply chains. The Chinese president proposed building "four key pillars" for development in the Asia-Pacific: economy and trade, connectivity, innovation and development.
He said China will provide $20 million to support cooperation in areas such as digital technology and clean energy.
9:50 a.m. Xi has opened the leaders summit, with the visiting dignitaries gathered around circular tables in a large conference room under chandeliers. Moments before sitting down for the plenary session, they took a photo with Xi in the center, flanked by Putin and Trump. Takaichi was positioned in the back row to the side.
9:40 a.m. In an interview with Fox News, Trump said he spoke with Xi about artificial intelligence, and former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang only came up "briefly," Reuters reports.
"I haven't heard that she was a spy," Trump said, in reference to Huang's extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.
9:30 a.m. APEC leaders are gathering for the forum's main event, which begins with a "family photo" before they convene for the plenary session. Xi has urged his guests to pursue "concrete results" promoting economic openness and innovation, but time is limited. Attention in the afternoon will turn to the U.S.-China bilateral meeting and the highly anticipated Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral. There are reports that Trump will squeeze in a one-on-one meeting with Putin as well, although it is unclear how substantial that would be.

articles.title_zh: Mideast nations ramp up efforts to avert all-out war as Israel urges Iran strikes, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The US has carried out further strikes on Iran despite Donald Trump ’s claim that the war is “effectively over” following his humiliating defeat in the midterm elections.
A fighter ⁠aircraft ‌targeted a missile launch site ‌on Qeshm ‌Island after Iran previously struck American personnel and assets in Bahrain, Reuters reported, citing US officials.
Tehran on Wednesday retaliated to US strikes on Qeshm by launching air attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait, the defence ministries of the two Arab nations said. It was Iran’s third strike on American military targets in Bahrain in five days.
Bahrain issued two alerts on Wednesday, urging residents to move to the nearest safe location, before announcing an all-clear after each warning.
It accused Iran ⁠of maintaining a "systematic hostile approach" of targeting the country, which hosts the US navy's Fifth Fleet.
Kuwait said its air defences were countering hostile drone attacks early on Wednesday, without ​providing further details.
Later in the morning, the Iranian army confirmed that it had targeted American drone and missile installations ⁠at ​Kuwait's ⁠Ali Al Salem ⁠base.
The attacks and counterattacks interrupted a roughly two-month lull in fighting and came just days after the US president declared the conflict “effectively over” and played down concerns that he would escalate after the elections.
Mr Trump had signalled Washington would hold off on ordering fresh strikes on Iran, provided there were no new attacks from Tehran or Yemen’s Houthi rebels .
“At this point, taking the military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing – but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason,” he told reporters at the White House .
A US official told the Associated Press that Washington used “precision munitions” to strike Qeshm Island in response to the “aggression” towards US personnel. Mr Trump, who is in the Philippines for the Asean summit, told reporters: “We are doing very well in Iran.”
The US carried out limited strikes on Qeshm earlier ⁠this month. Asked for comment, the US military’s Central Command said it had no updates.
Despite the fresh escalation, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on Wednesday he did not think there was any imminent threat to the US capital, dismissing a CNN report on the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington.
Mr Trump said the US was ​taking seriously ⁠the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack, while Iran’s foreign ministry denied the “baseless” allegations.
"I am ⁠not," Mr Rubio said when asked if he was concerned about ​an "imminent ⁠attack" on Washington. "I don't think there is ‌any imminent threat."
Mr Rubio added that the US government was "always on the lookout for anything that's a threat to the safety and security of the United States”.
Diplomatic efforts to end the war and open the Strait of Hormuz have been at a standstill despite the efforts of mediators from Pakistan and Qatar.
But Qatari and Iranian officials were meeting on Tuesday, Qatar said, as part of efforts to mediate an end to the nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East and pushed up global energy prices.
On Sunday, Tehran launched drone attacks on a US military base in Bahrain , following a similar strike on Friday.
Earlier this week, the US deployed a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt , to the Middle East, signalling a potential resumption of hostilities.
The American midterm election results proved devastating for the Republican Party, as voters expressed anger over soaring prices sparked by the unpopular conflict, which was prompted by joint US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran on 28 February.
The US president said officials were taking seriously the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a so-called dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign “to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs” using “baseless allegations”.
Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab.

articles.title_orig: Musk says he felt 'pretty foolish' about scale of midterm spending after Republican rout
articles.title_zh: Musk says he felt 'pretty foolish' about scale of midterm spending after Republican rout
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.
The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor , giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.
Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.
Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.
The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.
Musk was speaking virtually at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.
"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.
He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."
This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.
"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.
For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.
In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.
Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.
The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.
Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.
In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings , as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.
Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.
One of the most striking midterms wins went to Democrat James Talarico, who beat Republican Ken Paxton for a US Senate seat in Texas.
According to BBC analysis , Musk had spent at least $45m in support of Paxton.
Texas is where key operations for Musk's car company Tesla and rocket and technology firm SpaceX are based.
Musk said on Wednesday that he believes Texas' new governor, Democrat Gina Hinojosa, is "going to be quite moderate".
Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott, ending more than three decades of the party's control of the state.
The Tesla boss added : "I don't think she's a far-left governor. And based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, November 18, 2026: Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors’ Nerves
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, November 18, 2026: Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors’ Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”
